description: We are interested in developing solutions to potential real-world problems, primarily related to Earth's ecosystems. I am passionate about everything related to data science, web application development that solves critical issues, and working with tools that enable the creation of new solutions.
summary: We built an interactive web application in R Shiny that projects and visualizes the future potential distribution of the Pacific sardine (Sardinops sagax) off the California coast under contrasting climate scenarios. Users can choose between two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways—the sustainable SSP1-1.9 ("The Green Pathway") and the high-emission SSP5-8.5 ("Fossil-fueled Development")—and pick specific decades between 2050 and 2090 to generate interpolated habitat suitability maps, with direct downloads available in CSV and GeoTIFF formats. This project directly tackles the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge by filtering four critical oceanographic variables from climate models—sea surface temperature, salinity, chlorophyll-a, and mixed layer depth—to evaluate how, where, and by how much environmental conditions shift over time using a Random Forest model trained on historical California Cooperative Oceanic Fisheries Investigations records, pinpointing ecologically meaningful changes. Its value lies in the fact that Sardinops sagax is an ecological cornerstone of pelagic food webs and a vital fishery resource; anticipating its geographic shifts is essential to safeguarding food security, sustaining the fishing economy, and designing adaptive management measures in a warming ocean.
details:
Our project is an interactive web platform designed to explore how the potential habitat of the Pacific sardine (Sardinops sagax) will change over the course of the twenty-first century in California waters. Specifically, the application features a control panel where users choose between two contrasting IPCC climate scenarios—SSP1-1.9 and SSP5-8.5—and select a decadal time slice (2050, 2060, 2070, 2080, or 2090). Once the prediction and spatial interpolation run, the system dynamically displays the species potential distribution map and lets users directly download both the tabular data in CSV format and the spatial raster layers in GeoTIFF format for further analysis in geographic information systems.

To generate these projections, we trained a Random Forest machine learning algorithm using historical presence and absence records of sardine larvae collected during California Cooperative Oceanic Fisheries Investigations (CalCOFI) oceanographic cruises, georeferenced by latitude and longitude. The model integrated four oceanographic variables critical for spawning and larval survival: sea surface temperature, salinity, chlorophyll-a concentration, and mixed layer depth. Once calibrated and validated against historical records, the model was fed future projections of these exact same four oceanographic variables for each decade and socioeconomic pathway, producing continuous probability-of-presence surfaces through spatial interpolation.

The impact and benefits of this tool span both environmental and socioeconomic dimensions. By offering spatially explicit forecasts, the platform supports government agencies and the fishing sector in making adaptive management decisions, such as adjusting catch quotas or designing dynamic seasonal closures. This directly contributes to the sustainability of the small pelagic fishing industry, the preservation of coastal and oceanic food webs that rely on this forage species, and the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals tied to food security and marine conservation.

For technical development, we relied on open-source tools and collaborative environments: we used RStudio for statistical processing and training the Random Forest model, Google Colab to download satellite imagery of the climate variables, Visual Studio Code for code editing and structuring, QGIS for cartographic validation and spatial layer handling, and the R Shiny package to build and deploy the interactive web interface. The creativity of the project lies in democratizing complex ecological models, closing the gap between oceanographic data science and end users through a lightweight, visual, and exportable tool. Regarding design factors, we prioritized accessibility and lower operating costs by working exclusively with open-source software, optimizing the workflow so the application could run and deploy smoothly on standard computing hardware without requiring expensive server infrastructure.
